basic_identification.name: Collective intelligence infrastructure
basic_identification.originator: Systemic gap. No organization builds collective intelligence infrastructure specifically for the digital art field. Related efforts: ACM Collective Intelligence Conference (academic), DISCOLI workshop (distributed CI), Polis/vTaiwan (civic CI), Wikipedia/Wikidata (general knowledge), A(DAI) project (explicitly targeting this gap for digital art)
basic_identification.year: The concept of collective intelligence has academic lineage from the 1990s (Pierre Levy). The specific gap for digital art field knowledge aggregation has been recognized informally since the NFT boom revealed how fragmented field knowledge is (2021-present)
basic_identification.key_url: No single URL — this is a structural absence. Related: https://ci.acm.org/ (ACM CI conference), https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/26339137251328909 (AI for CI, 2025)
basic_identification.geography: Global gap. Individual knowledge exists everywhere practitioners work. No mechanism aggregates it across geographies. The gap is most acute at the intersections between local scenes and global field discourse.

core_ideas.core_claim: The digital art field has no mechanism to synthesize what it collectively knows. Individual practitioners hold deep knowledge about their scenes, practices, tools, markets, and communities — but this knowledge stays individual. It is never aggregated, structured, or made navigable at field scale. The field cannot answer basic questions about itself: How many generative artists are active globally? What preservation approaches are working? Which scenes are emerging? What aesthetic tendencies are forming? The deepest infrastructure gap is not about any specific function (funding, preservation, criticism) but about the absence of a system that could integrate knowledge across all functions.
core_ideas.medium_specificity: Digital art is uniquely suited for collective intelligence infrastructure because: (1) practitioners are digitally native and comfortable with online collaboration, (2) the field's artifacts are themselves digital and can be programmatically analyzed, (3) blockchain infrastructure already creates structured records (albeit only for ownership), and (4) the field is young enough that its knowledge has not yet calcified into institutional silos. Despite these advantages, no collective intelligence system exists.
core_ideas.relation_to_attention_economy: The attention economy actively fragments field knowledge. Platform algorithms create information silos: Twitter/X discourse is separate from marketplace data, which is separate from institutional programming, which is separate from practitioner experience. Each silo captures attention within its boundaries but prevents synthesis across boundaries. Collective intelligence infrastructure would counter this by creating cross-silo synthesis.
core_ideas.relation_to_intention: This is the deepest intention-aligned need. Collective intelligence infrastructure would serve the field's most fundamental structural requirement: self-knowledge. Without it, the field cannot act intentionally at scale — it cannot identify its gaps, coordinate its efforts, or build on its collective experience. Every other gap identified in this research (preservation, criticism, funding, scene documentation, meaning provenance) would be partially addressed by collective intelligence infrastructure that could identify, track, and coordinate responses to these gaps.

market_economics.revenue_model: No revenue model exists for digital art collective intelligence. Adjacent models: Wikipedia (donations + endowment), academic conferences (registration fees + institutional sponsorship), Dune Analytics/Nansen (subscription for on-chain analytics, but limited to market data). A(DAI) is exploring commons-first models that do not depend on subscription or advertising revenue.
market_economics.market_position: Infrastructure — the deepest layer, underlying all other market functions. Collective intelligence is not a market participant but a precondition for informed market activity.
market_economics.volume_trend_2024_2026: Growing in academic attention (ACM CI Conference series, DISCOLI workshop, Riedl & De Cremer 2025 paper on AI for CI). Growing in civic technology (Polis, deliberative democracy platforms). But no growth in digital art-specific collective intelligence infrastructure. A(DAI) represents the only known attempt to build this specifically for the digital art field. [uncertain]
market_economics.collector_demographics: Not applicable directly. However, all field participants — artists, collectors, curators, critics, institutions — would benefit from collective intelligence infrastructure that makes field knowledge navigable.
market_economics.sustainability: Unsolved. Collective intelligence infrastructure requires perpetual maintenance, moderation, and development. Wikipedia's endowment model is one precedent. Community-maintained open-source models are another. A(DAI)'s sustainability model is still being developed. The fundamental challenge: CI infrastructure is a public good that benefits everyone but is funded by no one.

practice_aesthetics.toolchain: Potential tools from adjacent domains: knowledge graphs (Neo4j, Wikibase), semantic web standards (RDF, SPARQL, LOD), collaborative platforms (MediaWiki, Notion), deliberation tools (Polis, Loomio), AI-assisted synthesis (NLP for extracting structured knowledge from unstructured text), on-chain data analysis (Dune Analytics, Flipside). No integrated toolchain exists for digital art collective intelligence.
practice_aesthetics.relation_to_AI: AI is potentially transformative for collective intelligence: it could aggregate dispersed knowledge, identify patterns across fragmented sources, translate between languages, and surface connections invisible to individual observers. Research by Riedl and De Cremer (2025) identifies three CI ingredients AI can support: collective memory, collective attention, and collective reasoning. However, AI also risks: homogenizing diverse perspectives, amplifying biases in training data, creating false confidence in synthesized knowledge, and deskilling community members who rely on AI rather than developing their own understanding.
practice_aesthetics.liveness: Collective intelligence is inherently live — it must evolve as the field evolves. Static knowledge bases become outdated. The challenge is designing systems that are continuously updated through community contribution while maintaining quality and coherence.
practice_aesthetics.aesthetic_vocabulary: Collective intelligence infrastructure must accommodate the field's diverse and evolving aesthetic vocabularies rather than imposing a single framework. This requires flexible ontologies that can incorporate multiple ways of describing and categorizing practice.
practice_aesthetics.tendency_axis_position: Maximally commons-oriented. Collective over individual (by definition). Infrastructure over spectacle (invisible foundational work). Openness over enclosure (shared knowledge is the entire point). The most commons-radical position on all tendency axes.

infrastructure_governance.openness: Must be radically open. Collective intelligence infrastructure is a commons resource that loses its purpose if enclosed. Open data, open source, open contribution pathways. However, openness must be balanced with quality control — not all contributions are equally valid.
infrastructure_governance.governance_model: Unsolved and critical. Potential models: wiki-style (community self-governance with admin layer), DAO (token-weighted governance), expert-committee (curatorial authority), deliberative (structured community decision-making). Each has trade-offs. Wiki-style scales but has quality issues. DAO governance can be captured by large token holders. Expert committees are high quality but do not scale. Deliberative models are thorough but slow. A(DAI) is exploring hybrid approaches.
infrastructure_governance.data_sovereignty: Community-controlled. Collective intelligence infrastructure must not be extractable by any single entity. Data should be portable, forkable, and governed by the community that creates it. This is a non-negotiable design requirement that rules out proprietary platforms.
infrastructure_governance.interoperability: Essential. Collective intelligence infrastructure must connect to: on-chain data (marketplace activity, ownership records), institutional databases (museum collections, exhibition records), critical publications (reviews, essays), community platforms (social media, forums), and other knowledge systems (Wikidata, academic databases). API-first design is required.
infrastructure_governance.preservation_strategy: Git-first (as A(DAI) proposes) provides version control and redundancy. Additional preservation through distributed storage, institutional partnerships, and periodic archival snapshots. The intelligence itself must be durably preserved — it represents the field's collective memory.
infrastructure_governance.consent_architecture: Must be granular and machine-readable. Contributors should control how their knowledge is used, attributed, and shared. Subjects (artists, organizations, scenes) should have voice in how they are represented. Consent should be opt-in for contribution and granular for attribution. This is a design challenge that no existing collective intelligence system has fully solved.

field_position.relation_to_traditional_art_world: The traditional art world has distributed collective intelligence in the form of: museum collections, exhibition histories, art historical scholarship, auction records, gallery networks, and critic communities. But this intelligence is fragmented across institutions and not computationally accessible. Digital art has less institutional knowledge and even less aggregation infrastructure.
field_position.what_it_enables: Collective intelligence infrastructure would enable: field-wide situation awareness (what is happening across the field), gap identification (what is missing or underserved), coordination (directing resources to identified needs), pattern recognition (identifying emerging tendencies before they become obvious), historical perspective (understanding the field's development over time), and democratic access to field knowledge (reducing information asymmetry between insiders and newcomers).
field_position.what_it_lacks: Everything. No technical system, no community practices, no governance model, no funding model, no contribution pathways, no quality control mechanisms, no integration standards. A(DAI) is the only known attempt to build this from scratch for the digital art field.
field_position.who_is_excluded: Currently: everyone, because the infrastructure does not exist. When built, risks of exclusion include: non-English speakers (if the system defaults to English), non-technical users (if contribution requires technical skills), practitioners without platform presence (if the system only ingests platform-visible signals), and minority perspectives (if governance does not protect against majority domination).
field_position.frontier_signal: Deep frontier. This is the most ambitious and least-developed infrastructure need in the field. Adjacent fields (civic technology, open-source software, academic research) have partial models. A(DAI) represents frontier experimentation in applying collective intelligence principles specifically to the digital art field.

attention_intention.discovery_mechanism: The concept of collective intelligence is discoverable through academic research (ACM CI Conference), technology publications, and civic technology discourse. The specific application to digital art is discoverable only through A(DAI) project communications and occasional critical discourse about field infrastructure gaps.
attention_intention.attention_dependency: Zero by design. Collective intelligence infrastructure should function regardless of platform attention dynamics. It creates value through knowledge aggregation, not engagement metrics.
attention_intention.intention_alignment: Maximally intention-aligned. This is pure intentional infrastructure — it serves the field's deepest structural need for collective self-knowledge. It has zero attention-capture function. It is the infrastructure that would make all other intentional activity more effective.
attention_intention.commons_contribution: The maximum possible commons contribution. A functioning collective intelligence system for digital art would be the single most valuable resource the field could build. It would transform every other field activity by providing shared situational awareness, historical context, and coordination capacity.

provenance_temporality.provenance_type: Collective intelligence infrastructure would track both meaning provenance (contextual, interpretive, relational history of works and practitioners) and meta-provenance (who contributed what knowledge, when, from what perspective). It would be the system within which meaning provenance lives.
provenance_temporality.temporal_logic: Multi-temporal. Must accommodate: real-time signals (current events, new work), cyclical patterns (market cycles, seasonal programming), deep historical context (decades of digital art history), and anticipatory analysis (emerging tendencies, future needs). A(DAI)'s bi-temporal model (event time + observation time) is an appropriate approach.
provenance_temporality.absence_handling: This IS the infrastructure for detecting and addressing absences. A functioning collective intelligence system would make visible what is missing from the field — undocumented scenes, unpreserved works, unfunded practices, unwritten criticism. Absence detection is a core function, not an edge case.

coherence.coherence_vs_consensus: Must produce coherence, never consensus. Multiple valid perspectives on the field should coexist and be navigable. The system should reveal the field's actual complexity and diversity, not flatten it into a single narrative. Coherence means: you can navigate across different perspectives and understand how they relate. Consensus means: one perspective dominates. The former is the goal.
coherence.contestability: Must be deeply and structurally contestable. Every claim, classification, and relationship in the system should be attributable, datable, and challengeable. Dissent should be preserved alongside consensus. Minority perspectives should be surfaceable, not buried. Contestability is a feature, not a bug — it ensures the system remains honest about the limits of its knowledge.
coherence.forkability: Must be fully forkable. Open data, open source, portable formats. Any community should be able to take the dataset and build their own intelligence layer on top of it. This is both an ethical requirement (preventing lock-in) and a practical one (forks can explore alternative organizing principles).

adai_comparison.what_adai_should_adopt: This IS what A(DAI) is building. A(DAI) should adopt: Git-first architecture for knowledge storage, Linked Open Data for interoperability, bi-temporal modeling for temporal depth, community contribution pathways for knowledge ingestion, tendency-based analysis for identifying field dynamics, scene-level documentation as a core knowledge layer, and meaning provenance as the interpretive complement to ownership records.
adai_comparison.what_adai_should_refuse: A(DAI) should refuse: platform dependency (build on open infrastructure, not proprietary platforms), extractive knowledge gathering (knowledge should benefit contributors, not just consumers), consensus-forcing (preserve disagreement and diversity), AI-only synthesis (human judgment must remain central), and premature formalization (leave room for knowledge that resists categorization).
adai_comparison.structural_tension: A(DAI) attempts to build collective intelligence through centralized infrastructure (a single knowledge graph, a single sensing loop). But collective intelligence is inherently distributed — it emerges from many independent actors. The tension is between the need for coherent infrastructure (which requires some centralization) and the distributed nature of the intelligence it aims to capture. A(DAI) must be centralized enough to be navigable but distributed enough to capture genuine diversity.

regulatory_legal.regulatory_exposure: GDPR and data protection regulations apply to any system that stores information about identifiable individuals (practitioners, curators, critics). EU AI Act may apply if AI is used for synthesis or classification of cultural data. Copyright law applies to aggregation of published texts. Data scraping regulations vary by jurisdiction. No specific regulation addresses cultural collective intelligence systems, creating both freedom and uncertainty.
regulatory_legal.ip_model: Must be open by design. Contributed knowledge should be licensed under open terms (CC-BY or CC-BY-SA). Aggregated data should be available under open data licenses. Proprietary enclosure of collective intelligence defeats its purpose. However, respecting the IP of source materials (critical texts, institutional records) requires careful licensing and fair use analysis.
regulatory_legal.opt_in_vs_opt_out: Contribution should be opt-in. Inclusion as a subject should follow established norms (public figures and public works are documented without consent; private information requires consent). Machine-readable consent frameworks should be built into the architecture.

ecosystem.platform_dependency: Must be platform-independent by design. Build on open infrastructure (Git, open-source databases, open standards). Current field knowledge is scattered across platform-dependent channels — collective intelligence infrastructure must extract and aggregate from these while not depending on any single one.
ecosystem.network_effects: Potentially the strongest network effects of any infrastructure in the field. Every contribution makes the system more valuable for all participants. Knowledge aggregation is a classic positive-sum network good. The challenge is reaching the critical mass needed to activate these effects — early-stage collective intelligence systems face the cold-start problem.
ecosystem.post_crash_trajectory: The 2022-2023 crash revealed the consequences of absent collective intelligence: the field could not coordinate responses to market collapse, practitioners lacked shared situational awareness, and recovery efforts were fragmented and uncoordinated. Post-crash: growing recognition that the field needs shared infrastructure for self-knowledge. A(DAI) launched in this context. Academic interest in collective intelligence for cultural domains is growing. But the gap between recognition and implementation remains vast.
